content: Portulaca oleracea, commonly referred to as Common Purslane, Verdolaga, Pigweed, Little Hogweed, or Pusley, is an annual succulent plant belonging to the family Portulacaceae. It can grow up to 40 cm in height. This plant is native to India and the Middle East but has become naturalized in other regions. In some areas, it is considered an invasive weed. However, evidence from Crawford Lake deposits in Ontario, dating back to 1430–1489, suggests that this species may have reached North America during the pre-Columbian era. The plant features smooth, reddish stems that are mostly prostrate, with alternate leaves clustered at stem joints and ends. Its yellow flowers, which are approximately 6 mm wide, have five regular parts. These flowers begin to bloom in late spring and continue until mid-fall. They open individually at the center of leaf clusters for only a few hours on sunny mornings. The seeds are produced in small pods that open when the seeds are mature. Purslane has a taproot with fibrous secondary roots and is highly tolerant of poor, compacted soils and drought conditions. Culinary Usage Although Purslane is often regarded as a weed in the United States, it is edible and consumed as a leafy vegetable. It has a slightly sour and salty flavor and is widely eaten across Europe and Asia. It can be used fresh in salads, cooked like spinach, or incorporated into soups and stews due to its mucilaginous properties. Australian Aboriginals historically used its seeds to make seed cakes. Purslane is notable for its high content of Omega-3 fatty acids, containing more than any other leafy vegetable. Specifically, it has been reported to contain 0.1 mg/g of eicosapentaenoic acid (EPA), a type of Omega-3 fatty acid typically found in fish and some algae. Additionally, Purslane is rich in vitamins, particularly vitamin C, some B vitamins, and carotenoids, as well as dietary minerals such as magnesium, calcium, potassium, and iron. The plant also contains two types of betalain alkaloid pigments: reddish betacyanins, which are visible in the coloration of the stems, and yellow betaxanthins, which are noticeable in the flowers and the slight yellowish tint of the leaves. Both pigment types are potent antioxidants and have demonstrated antimutagenic properties in laboratory studies. Medicinal Usage In Greek traditional medicine, Purslane is used as a remedy for constipation and inflammation of the urinary system. History Purslane has been widely utilized in Greece, with archaeobotanical evidence of its use found at numerous prehistoric sites. In historical contexts, seeds have been recovered from a protogeometric layer in Kastanas and from the Samian Heraion, dating back to the 7th century BCE. In North India, where it is known as Sanhti or Punarnava, Purslane is recognized for its role as a liver tonic and is used in the treatment of liver diseases.
